title: Cut squares, find the tile
hook: The biggest square tile for a 48 by 18 floor, found without listing a single factor.

knows: a rectangle can be covered by equal squares when both sides are multiples of the square's side
doesNotKnow: Euclid's repeated-cutting method for the greatest common divisor

misconception: Finding the biggest shared tile size needs guessing, or listing all the factors of both sides.
objective: The learner can explain that repeatedly cutting the biggest square off a rectangle ends on a square whose side is the biggest tile that covers the original exactly (the greatest common divisor).

claims.text: Cutting the biggest square off a 48 by 18 rectangle again and again cuts squares of 18, 18, 12 and 6 and leaves a 6 by 6 square.
claims.source: Recomputed with node; the stage's euclid() function produces the cuts and the chips' labels.

claims.text: The biggest square tile that covers a 48 by 18 floor exactly has side 6, and 8 by 3 = 24 of them cover it; 9 and 12 do not divide both sides.
claims.source: gcd(48, 18) = 6, recomputed with node; 48 / 9 and 18 / 12 are not whole numbers.

claims.text: A tile that fits a rectangle exactly also fits what is left after cutting off a square, and the last square left fits every piece, so it is the biggest shared tile.
claims.source: If t divides a and b it divides a - b; conversely the final side divides every earlier side by working back up. This is gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a - b).
Euclid, Elements VII.2 (finding the greatest common measure of two numbers).

recall.question: Cutting the biggest square off a 21 by 15 rectangle again and again, what square is left at the end?
recall.why: Cut 15 (leaves 6 by 15), cut 6 twice (leaves 6 by 3), cut 3 (leaves 3 by 3). So 3 is the biggest tile that fits both 21 and 15.
